title: Evidence for superconductivity at 190 K in a pressure-overdoped cuprate
authors: Alexander C. Mark, Huu T. Do, David Rodriguez, D. Gonzalez Arevalo, Adam Denchfield, Eduardo H. T. Poldi, Daniel P. Phelan, N. K. Man, Rssell J. Hemley
abstract: It is well established that the critical temperature ($T_c$) of cuprate superconductors can be tuned by pressure. For example, compression decouples the hole doping from chemical doping allowing for overdoped samples far beyond what is possible at ambient pressure. In this work, multiple techniques are used to probe the onset of the Meissner effect at $T_c$ as a function of pressure in $\mathrm{Pb_{0.4}Bi_{1.6}Sr_2Ca_2Cu_3O_{10+δ}}$ (Bi-2223) to 60 GPa in different compression environments. Samples compressed under quasihydrostatic conditions exhibit a distinctive non-monotonic pressure dependence of $T_c$ below 25 GPa, in agreement with previous reports. With further increase in pressure $T_c$ climbs continuously to 190 K at 60 GPa. Evidence for critical temperatures exceeding those reported to date for cuprates at ambient and high pressures, the results may be understood in terms of the proposed second superconducting regime at high hole doping.
summary: This study reports on measuring superconducting critical temperatures ($T_c$) in cuprates under extreme pressures up to 60 GPa. By combining advanced magnetic susceptibility measurements with DFT calculations, the authors demonstrate a continuous rise of $T_c$ to 190 K at high pressure. This suggests the existence of a 'second superconducting regime' driven by significant electronic restructuring at very high hole doping levels.
main_problem: The study investigates how applying high external pressure affects the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) in cuprate superconductors, specifically looking for evidence of a second superconducting regime at highly overdoped states.
main_result: The research reports observing $T_c$ rising continuously to 190 K at 60 GPa, suggesting that high pressure induces electronic restructuring leading to enhanced superconductivity beyond previously known limits.
method: A combination of experimental techniques (AC susceptibility, double modulation, RF susceptibility) under high-pressure diamond anvil cells, complemented by DFT calculations to model doping changes, was employed.
model_or_system: The physical system is the cuprate superconductor $	ext{Pb}_{0.4}	ext{Bi}_{1.6}	ext{Sr}_2	ext{Ca}_2	ext{Cu}_3	ext{O}_{10+\delta}$ ($	ext{Bi-2223}$). The theoretical framework involves modeling how pressure modifies the hole doping concentration ($n_H$) and induces changes in the Fermi surface topology.
key_observables: Meissner effect onset, $T_c$ dependence on pressure (up to 60 GPa), AC susceptibility ($\chi'$ and $\chi''$), and calculated equivalent hole doping ($n_H$).
important_parameters: Pressure range up to 60 GPa; critical temperature reaching 190 K; high hole doping regime.
main_assumptions: The interpretation relies on the assumption that pressure-induced changes in electronic structure (as modeled by DFT) govern the superconducting enhancement, and careful background subtraction is necessary for susceptibility measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate DAC setups, temperature dependence of magnetic susceptibility ($\chi'$), modulated signal amplitudes under different compression environments, and calculated hole doping ($n_H$) vs. pressure.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of pressure tuning in cuprates, presents experimental measurements across various high-pressure regimes using multiple susceptometry techniques, analyzes the non-monotonic behavior at lower pressures, and concludes by presenting evidence for a continuous rise to 190 K, linking it to a second superconducting regime.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses unconventional superconductivity in strongly correlated materials, which is a major focus area. The use of high pressure as an external tuning parameter provides a unique way to map out the phase diagram and explore exotic electronic states relevant to many-body physics.
